lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Launch and diagnostic: audience, tone, and register

objective: Learners read three short draft messages about the same scheduling situation, written for a friend, a coach, and a teacher, identify which register each uses and which one does not match its audience, then rewrite the mismatched message and name the specific wording changes that fixed the register.
scenario: The learner is given three short messages already drafted on this task sheet, one addressed to a friend, one to a coach, and one to a teacher, all about asking to move a practice or turn in work late. One message uses a register that does not fit its audience. The learner finds it, rewrites it, and explains the shift.
safetyNotes: All three messages on this task sheet are provided examples for analysis; none are sent to a real coach, teacher, or friend as part of this lesson.
materials: the three sample messages printed on this task sheet

tasks.directions: Read the three messages below, all about the same kind of situation. Message A: 'hey can we push practice to friday? sry for last min lol'. Message B: 'Hi Coach Diaz, would it be possible to move Thursday's practice to Friday? I have a scheduling conflict. Thank you.' Message C: 'hey mr thompson can i turn in the essay late lol my bad.' Decide which audience each message fits (a friend, a coach, or a teacher) based on its wording alone.

prompts.text: Which audience (friend, coach, or teacher) does each message's wording actually fit, and which one message is aimed at an audience its wording doesn't match?

tasks.directions: Rewrite Message C so its register fits a teacher, using a greeting with the teacher's name and title, no slang, a plainly stated request, and a polite closing with your name.

prompts.text: My rewrite opens with the teacher's name and an appropriate title instead of slang.
My rewrite removes casual abbreviations like 'lol' and 'my bad' and states the request in plain language.
My rewrite closes with a polite line and my name.

tasks.directions: Compare your rewrite of Message C to Message A, the friend message, even though both messages are making a similar kind of request.

prompts.text: Name three specific words or phrases you changed between the casual version and your teacher-register rewrite, and explain what register each version signals.

tasks.directions: Think about why register matters even when the underlying request is the same.

prompts.text: Explain one real situation where using the wrong register with a teacher or coach could hurt you, even if your request itself was reasonable.

remediation: If a learner cannot tell Message C is mismatched, have them circle every slang word or abbreviation in all three messages first, then sort messages by how many casual markers they contain before asking again which audience each fits — the mismatch becomes visible once the markers are counted.
extension: Have the learner write a fourth message for the same scheduling situation addressed to a school administrator they've never met, adjusting the register to be more formal than the coach message and explaining what made it more formal.
